<div class="notes">
  <article class="note" id="what-counts-as-intelligence">
    <p class="note__meta">
      <time datetime="2026-10-06T17:38:53-04:00">6 October 2026, EDT (UTC−04:00)</time>
    </p>
    <h2 class="note__title">What counts as intelligence?</h2>
    <p>I don't understand why people talk as if AI makes human intelligence irrelevant. Deriving equations and writing code matter, but what about handling several problems at once, learning quickly, and knowing which direction is worth pursuing? Don't these count as intelligence? I would call them a higher form of it, developed through broader experience than any single technical skill demands. These are exactly the abilities we need most when working with AI, whether in research or in making engineering ideas work.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="note" id="where-modeling-pays-off">
    <p class="note__meta">
      <time datetime="2026-09-28T18:45:34-04:00">28 September 2026, EDT (UTC−04:00)</time>
    </p>
    <h2 class="note__title">Where modeling pays off</h2>
    <p>Everyday robotics faces countless interactions, making a detailed model for every situation impractical. In science and engineering, the challenge can lie deep within a single system, where understanding one critical coupling is already a major advance. This changes what I want from physical intelligence: the ability to handle many situations, and the ability to resolve the dynamics that matter within one.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="note" id="from-language-to-reliable-control">
    <p class="note__meta">
      <time datetime="2026-09-09T18:06:06-04:00">9 September 2026, EDT (UTC−04:00)</time>
    </p>
    <h2 class="note__title">Scaling and physical generalization</h2>
    <p>I keep wondering whether scaling can give us physical generalization. Models can share representations and solvers, but different dynamics may still require different control laws. Perhaps a model can generalize by recognizing the regime and applying local rules, without discovering a unified physical theory. What would convince me is reliable control across unfamiliar systems without extensive reference trajectories or retraining. That would suggest a general mechanism for physical reasoning.</p>
  </article>
  <article class="note" id="emergence-and-physical-intelligence">
    <p class="note__meta">
      <time datetime="2026-09-07T11:40:00-04:00">7 September 2026, EDT (UTC−04:00)</time>
      <span>Ithaca, New York</span>
    </p>
    <h2 class="note__title">Emergence and physical intelligence</h2>
    <p>I do not expect physical intelligence to show the emergence reported for large language models. If a mechanism for wide transfer exists, it should come from structure rather than from parameter count, because the laws that govern a physical system have always turned out to be short.</p>
  </article>
</div>
